7.12.m:
And he who gives vessels completely filled, O fair-faced ones,
shall become a vessel of pleasures and rescues his ancestors from danger.
He who constructs an abundant pond of water, O goddesses,
where indeed all creatures drink water—
having delivered his fathers, and likewise grandfathers
and great-grandfathers, in desirable worlds,
[becoming] a bird, he roams like a god, O goddesses, for six hundred tens of thousands of years.
And again in the human world, free from all diseases,
he becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and is born on par with a king—
a giver, a sacrificer, strong, radiant, and handsome.
That man who digs a pit full of water, O fair-smiling ones,
and gives it to brahmins after having properly fed them,
adorned with eight varied banners,
and decorated with a flag, a streamer, and flowers—
having delivered his ancestors, that best of men,
goes by an aerial chariot praised in song by apsarases to the realm of Varuṇa.
Whoever gives silver, gold, land, sesame seeds, or jewels
to all beings, hear the fruit of his merit:
Accompanied by all worlds, in a great aerial chariot,
having reached the world of Indra, he rejoices like a god.
And having fallen thence, righteous and prosperous with all desires,
he is born in this world in a great family, fortunate indeed.
The man who plants a tree that yields shade, flowers, and fruit
along the path, O gentle goddesses, he delivers his ancestors.

7.12.m:
Likewise, having given it to brahmins and then redeemed it, a man—
what fruit he obtains, hear that, O splendid ones!
As long as embodied beings enjoy the blossoms of the tree
and the fruits of the bearing tree are eaten by creatures,
for that many thousands of years, having delivered even his ancestors,
he reaches the world of Soma and attains the immortal fruit.
He who attentively gives fruits to brahmins,
he shall become a possessor of many fruits and fortunate indeed.
The best among men who offers firewood in the winter season
to brahmins, O goddesses, he enjoys the world of Agni.
He who offers a golden vessel adorned with jewels
rejoices in heaven in an aerial chariot crowded with hundreds of apsarases.
He who offers a silver vessel to brahmins, O auspicious ones,
having reached the status of a gandharva, rejoices with Urvaśī.
He who gives a copper vessel especially to brahmins
becomes a yakṣa endowed with power in the service of the king of yakṣas.
He who presents a house filled with all desired things,
having attained the world of Brahmā, is served with all desires.
Having dwelt there for four full crores [of years] by that deed,
he is then born as a generous, pleasure-enjoying householder.
He who provides medicinal herbs and various grains
attains the world of Soma, adorned with all desires.
Having stayed there for seven thousand years, that man
is born here endowed with all wealth and enjoying pleasures.

7.12.m: And he who gives a water-cow, the fruit of his gift is great: / having set up an auspicious water-booth, a pond, or a fully abundant well, / having filled water-pitchers completely, adorned them with fragrant unguents and garlands / and diverse kinds of flowers, and having worshipped the best of brahmins, / thoroughly satisfied with food and drink, he should give them vessels of sesame seeds; / he should give an abundant priestly gift, and then make them touch it [saying]: / 'May the waters, auspicious and gentle, satisfy my ancestors; / may my ancestors always go where they will and grant all desires.' / Having thus given that cow and then bought it back, / he should maintain that water-booth, O goddess, which secures the world of Brahmā. / Having given vessels of sesame seeds, a pair of new garments, / the presence of gold, and diverse kinds of fruits, / he should then, pure and having taken a ritual ablution, give according to rule to the brahmins. / […] / 'Clarified butter the cows bring forth; clarified butter is established in the earth; / clarified butter is fire and the gods; may clarified butter be bestowed upon me.' / Giving according to this rule, he reaches the world of Brahmā. / The man who gives a cow along with her calf and a bronze milking pail, / with golden horns, silver hooves, draped in fine silk and linen, / furnished with a bed and covering, endowed with many flowers and fruits, / having gratified the brahmins, adorned with fragrant unguents and garlands— / at the time of the gift, the gods dwell within her limbs: / Brahmā resides on her head, Śakra rests upon her flank, / the moon and the sun are in her eyes, and the wind is established in her nostrils.

(25) / But having eaten on the tenth day, he obtains the fruit of a ten-day sacrifice; / becoming equal to the Aśvins, he constantly shines like the sun. (26) / And obtaining human birth again, he obtains ten wives, / imperishable gold, and he does not die untimely. (27)
The pure man who eats on the eleventh day, / having obtained the fruit of the eleventh [day], attains the state of a member of Rudra's retinue. (28)
Having stayed there for eight hundred [years], endowed with great happiness, / he obtains brahminhood and is born here as a performer of sacrifices. (29)
The man, O goddesses, who constantly eats on the twelfth day, / having obtained [the fruit of] a twelve-day rite, reaches Indra's world. (30)

And whatever woman, permitted by her husband, having performed abundant duty, / gives [the merit] to her husband, her fruit becomes infinite. // 72
And whatever she desires, either in this world or in the next, / she attains all that, O goddesses, and also becomes fortunate. // 73
Her husband becomes devoted to her, and she is dear to him then; / she has sons and offspring, and does not experience sorrow. // 74
This duty has been told by me to you, O mothers of the world. / What else do you wish to hear further than this, O beautiful ones? // 75

7.12.m:
[Sanatkumāra said:]
“Ah, the dharma has been declared by you, O lady revered by all the gods! / By the practice of which a very great fruit is quickly obtained. // 78
From here, O goddess, let us look upon the auspicious forest of this mountain, / strewn with kinds of flowers and filled with flocks of numerous birds.” // 79
Then, having arisen, that goddess, together with the mothers of the gods, / [set out] to see that excellent, divine forest of Mount Mandara. // 80
Endowed with great yoga, directing her eye that brings pleasant ease, she walked about, / beholding the peaks made of red arsenic and gold, // 81
and the delightful, clear-watered torrents of the mountain, / pools full of blue lotuses, and most charming reservoirs; / seeing these, and Nandin standing at her side, the Mountain's Daughter rejoiced. // 82
Then a slender-waisted daughter of Meru, named Śubhāvatī, / said to the daughter of Himavat, showing her the auspicious forest: // 83
“O Daughter of the Mountain, look at this [forest], beautiful with playful graces, / endowed with every season, like [...] well-spoken [wisdom]. // 84
This very great [mountain] brings forth [...] / like a well-spoken [counsel] applied by the wise in times of distress. // 85
So too shines the excellent golden rock on the mountain peak, / like a learned Sāmaveda chanter singing according to the rules. // 86
And this gem-studded, radiant mountain crest constantly / shines like the rising sun [...]. // 87
This beryl peak with a floor of sapphire / shines, O Śarvāṇī, bearing [...] over the mountain [...]. // 88
This intoxicated elephant, looking like one surrounded by female elephants, / bowing its head down, O fair-browed one, with its sprout [...] // 89 //”

“Ah, behold this handsome [tree] endowed with rows of woods, O auspicious lady, / like Jayanta anointed to the heir-apparentship with chowries! // 90
And behold this tree, O Śarvāṇī, dancing with its sprout-hands / beside its mother, like a dear son born of her own womb. // 91
Indeed, I consider this the beloved dwelling of the goddess of the forest; / an exceeding splendor is seen here such as I have never seen!” // 92
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of Śubhāvatī, the Mountain's Daughter, / the imperishable daughter of Himavat, looked upon the young tree. // 93
And so that goddess of gods, roaming on the great mountain, / saw a young aśoka tree in full bloom, radiant like the rising sun, // 94
standing with its hundreds of coppery sprouts joined as if in folded hands. / Having seen it, O sage, the goddess Girijā experienced supreme joy, // 95
and thought in her mind: “This tree is my son. / This praiseworthy son of mine will be an increaser of delight. // 96
When the Lord arrives, then, permitted by the Self-manifest [Śiva], / I will adopt this young aśoka tree as my dear son. // 97
And for me, who am childless, this best of trees will become / a son, O best of mothers, destroying the grief of [not having] a son.” // 98
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus decided about that tree, the beautiful Umā, / moving toward another place, looked about there. // 99
Then, in the meantime, terrible omens occurred there: / there arose a great velocity of wind that felled the mountain trees. // 100

A peak of the lord of mountains fell without any calamity, / and trees were uprooted without any wind. // 101
Meteors fell from the sky, and an inauspicious wind blew; / moreover, O delight of Kālī, the goddess’s left eye twitched. // 102

Andhaka said: / 'Who is this slender-waisted lady here, incomparable in beauty, auspicious? / Never before have I seen such a woman, O dānavas! // Look at this slender-waisted one who has come [either] in heaven or on earth! / If she is indeed a wife, whose is she, and who is her lord husband? // Who am I, and why do I live? This word of mine is true: / He whose youthful wife this is, possessing lovely, splendid, long eyes, // what need has that fortunate, great-souled one of dwelling in heaven? / This secret kingdom is false for me, as long as this woman is not my beloved!
I have many thousands of beautiful women; / they are all fit merely to be her handmaidens, O dānavas!'
Sanatkumāra said: / Hearing that speech of his, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, / embracing Andhaka, spoke many wonderful things, O son of Kālī:

With its ravines, ridges, caves, and mountain streams, / nothing more delightful than it exists anywhere on earth. // 134
Then all those demon lords roamed upon the great mountain, / which was filled with many cascades and crowded with diverse trees. // 135
Roaming there, they saw the seven seers, great sages endowed with yoga, / perfected masters staying at a certain mountain stream, // 136
seated upon a stone slab, conversing with one another / in tales full of righteousness, of wondrous import, insightful, and bringing great joy. // 137
Seeing them, that Andhaka questioned Prahlāda, the foremost of the asuras: / “Who are these seers here, and for what purpose have they gathered here?” // 138
Then the wise asura, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, having understood, / positioned in their midst, spoke to that thorn in the side of the gods. // 139
Prahlāda said:
“O Andhaka, these are the seven great-souled seers who have assembled: / Bhṛgu, Atri, Marīci, Viśvāmitra, and Aṅgiras, // 140
as well as Bharadvāja and Vasiṣṭha—masters of yoga whose wealth is austerity, / great-souled men whose sins are burnt away by austerity, who have come here. // 141
I do not think their arrival at Mandara is without cause, O lord. / Remaining here in seclusion from this point, let us, all the lords of the asuras, // find out what work these adepts are doing here. // 142
Becoming quiet, holding their peace, according to their strength, / let us learn the opinion of all of them; remain silent, O lords of the daityas!” // 143

Then, having made an agreement, those bulls among the asuras stood by: / “Whoever among us utters a sound shall be put to death by us.” // 144
While those wicked-minded asuras stood thus, / those seers endowed with austerity spoke words to one another: // 145
“This region of the mountain is not pure; today let us go elsewhere, O twice-born ones! / For the arrival of very wicked daityas is seen here. // 146
Even Bhavānī has gone elsewhere, distressed by the fear of the asuras. / Those asuras are wicked-souled, whose destruction is certain. // 147
All those who destroy righteousness have gone to their doom. / If those cruel ones had not destroyed righteousness for the sake of kingdom, // 148
those haters of the gods would not all have met their destruction in this manner. / If they had remained contented with their own realm, // they too would have shone in all the worlds, worthy of worship like the gods.” // 149
Sanatkumāra said:
Aṅgiras said this to them: “Indeed, there is no [lasting joy] here for those who desire; / for those who have set out for the sake of dominion, unrighteousness is close at hand. // 150
Righteousness alone indeed secures a kingdom for the desirous; / one should never practice unrighteousness; [in it] there is no stability or realm whatsoever.” // 151
Atri said:
“They desire a kingdom through unrighteousness, and they constantly conquer in battle, / but those whose livelihood harms others do not become dear to the world. // 152

7.12.m:
The righteous, on the other hand, soon slay their enemies without agitation / and become firmly established in their kingdoms; therefore one should take refuge in righteousness. // 153
Those, however, who, abandoning righteousness and delighting in wickedness, / seek a kingdom by sheer force, do not ever attain that kingdom. // 154
And whatever kingdom is attained by them through cruel deeds, / that does not belong to them for long, and they become hated on that account.” // 156
Bhṛgu said:
“In ancient times, this righteousness, which brings fear to the asuras, / was attained by Brahmā wishing to create, but they do not abide by it. // 157
By their very nature, they are all cruel from birth; / and because of their cruel inclination, they have resorted to that conduct.” // 158
Sanatkumāra said:
While they were conversing in this manner regarding the asuras, / the three arrived: Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Kṛtānta. // 159
Having duly honoured them, devoted to one another, / those seers as well as those three sat down upon the stones. // 160
The seers bowed with great respect to those who were seated / and said: “Where have you, the sustainers of the world, set out for today?” // 161
Dhātṛ said:
“Returning from the world of Brahmā today, we have come, O twice-born ones; / we have been commanded by Brahmā to go near Kaśyapa.” // 162

7.12.m: Again the sages asked, “What was told to Kaśyapa, the twice-born?” / Then Dhātṛ related to the sages what he had told Kaśyapa: // “When you informed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, O brāhmaṇa, [saying,] / ‘The asuras are my sons, and the gods are also dear to me, O Lord. // Act in such a way, O best of immortals, that they do not harbor mutual enmity, / O creator of the world, so that I may then be at peace.’ // Commanded there by Brahmā, I say unto you, O great sage: / As the conduct of gods and asuras, and their mutual friendship, // and the production of nectar, and the kingdom and the establishment of all order— / having been asked by you, O best of seers, the Lord narrated / everything of the future deeds of the gods and asuras. // Having reported all that to him, we were sent by Brahmā / and have come here to see the Lady, the daughter of the snowy mountain.” // Sanatkumāra said: / To those who spoke thus, those seers rich in tapas, / with restrained minds, all asked again then, O sage: // “What conduct of the gods and asuras is told to happen in the future, O auspicious ones, / that we wish to hear, if your mind is inclined to favor us. // And what did you report to the goddess, O best of gods? / Narrate all that as well, if we indeed deserve your favor.” // Hearing their words, those three best of gods, / endowed with great might, said to him: “You explain it, O Kṛtānta!”

Vyāsa said: / What was told of old to those seers on Mandara by that great-souled Kṛtānta, / narrate all that to me.
Sanatkumāra said: / There will be a son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, / Indra of the asuras, mighty, wise, Prahlāda, the bull among asuras. // Having produced nectar along with the gods, the leader of the host of gods, / having conquered the gods in battle, that bull among Daityas took the nectar away; / then, defeated in battle by Viṣṇu, he will consecrate his son to the kingdom.
Vyāsa said: / How was that nectar churned by the gods / and the mighty asuras, O son of Brahmā? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said: / When Prahlāda, the bull among asuras, was consecrated in Indra’s realm / by Brahmā, O Vyāsa, he then protected the asuras. // Then there was a battle of the gods with the asuras. / The gods then addressed the venerable Grandfather.
The gods said: / “Lord, the gods are slain in battle by the asuras like mortals! / Direct us, O you of noble vows, so that the gods do not die!”

7.12.m:
Addressed thus, Brahmā said to the gods with Indra: / “Go and quickly produce nectar from the Ocean of Milk. // In all the manvantaras, whichever gods arise, / all of them produce nectar from the Ocean of Milk together with the asuras. // Then the lords of the gods consume it, and from that satisfaction arises; / even the dead rise up, and having drunk it, they do not die.”
The gods said: / “How do the gods, the lords of the manvantaras, / produce that nectar on earth? Tell us that entire means.”
Brahmā said: / “In the western region, in Somapurī, is that auspicious lake, the Ocean of Milk, / where those seven auspicious oceans are always present; // where Irā, Mālā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, Irāvatī, / Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Surabhi, and Kadrū, // Aditi, Diti, and Devikā, the source of all things, / and the all-enduring, auspicious cows that grant all desires, // affectionate, yield six-flavored milk comparable to nectar; / where dwell the foam-drinking seers, whose nature is austerity, restraint, and tranquility. // Gathering whatever herbs exist in this world, O best of gods, / domestic, wild, celestial, and human by the thousands, // trees, creepers, shrubs, bushes, and other such plants, / and casting in medicaments, and King Soma,

Strength, righteousness, energy, contentment, the goddess Sarasvatī,
all the sacred fords, and diverse gifts,
the bull, the chariot, the banner, the elephant, and the horse,
and eight auspicious things they cast there, as well as the Vedic metres,
the Vedas, whatever knowledges there be, and these Mothers of the Worlds,
mantras, sacrifices, gold, and the ritual utensils of mantras;
throwing whatever was splendid, satisfying, and full of sap therein,
they then brought the churning rod:
Mandara, the foremost of mountains, and Akūpāra the tortoise.
Having placed the churning rod, Mandara the lord of mountains, upon its back,
held firm by Viṣṇu, and Vāsuki as the churning-rope—
where his head was, there were the Daityas; where his tail was, there were the gods—
pulling that churning rod, they churned for many years.
Then, after a thousand years, a horse shall rise up from it.

7.12.m:
[Apparatus readings]
"Thus in the Manvantaras here, by the gods together with Asuras and humans,
nectar is churned, O gods, and in that manner it is produced.
Therefore, going hence together with the Dānavas, O deities,
churn the nectar quickly; then you shall obtain that benefit."
Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed thus by Brahmā, the creator of the world, those lords of the gods
returned to this world and acted accordingly in every respect.
While it was being churned, poison arose first,
terrifying to gods and Asuras; Śaṅkara then drank it.
Then, once again, from that ocean of milk there arose
many wondrous treasures; the deities took them.
The Asuras did not take them, and those [treasures] cursed the Asuras;
they despised the auspicious things, and because of that they met destruction.
The treasures said:
"Since you wicked, cruel ones do not rejoice in us,
therefore whatever you desire shall not come to pass in that way."
The Asuras did not even take Vāruṇī, who brings intoxication and power;
therefore, those Asuras were indeed wicked in every way.
Then arose the horse named Uccaiḥśravas, supremely splendid,
and the four-tusked elephant, and the physician of very great fame,
Ghṛtācī, Pūrvacitti, and the enchanting divine Rambhā;
and taking the nectar, Soma then arose, O gods.

[Apparatus readings]
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having abandoned those treasures, the excessively arrogant Asuras
then seized the nectar by sheer force from the hand of Soma.
The gods, approaching them together, spoke with soothing words to them who were deluded:
"It is not proper for you to act thus; let us partake of it together.
May our friendship be very firm! Filled with the pride of strength,
do not make this toil futile here, O lords of the Dānavas!"
To all of them speaking thus, Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas,
a master of great illusions, setting righteousness aside, said this:
Prahlāda said:
"When you took the treasures that arose from the ocean,
at that time nothing was said to you by us, O lords of the gods!
In this same way we, all the gods [here], take this treasure;
we will certainly not give this up today without a fight.
This nectar, the source of all auspiciousness, has come into our hands, O gods;
if you must have it, take it by battle if you can!"
Sanatkumāra said:
Spoken to thus by those cruel ones, the gods were as if frightened;
pale-faced and dejected, they said nothing to them at that time.
Embarrassed by that, the lords of the gods, being of great courage, turned away;
they indeed became dispirited, thinking, "We are ruined!"
Seeing them thinking thus, Purandara of a thousand eyes
said: "What is the use of despair? Let us slay them in battle!"

7.12.m:
The Bālakhilyas said:
That which was spoken by you as “Blue-throated”, O best of winds, / that we wish to hear, by your grace, O wind-god! / How did the blueness of Ambikā's lord's throat come about? / We wish to hear it thoroughly, especially from your mouth. / This is meritorious, that which [is heard] by us; for that is our supreme welfare. / Whatever utterances proceed, all of them indeed are impelled by you. / When the wind reaches the place of articulation, the operation of speech proceeds; / knowledge, discernment, and energy proceed from you, O wind! / […] by the application, all phonemes are set forth, / from which words turn back and are hard to obtain, bound in the body. / Even there, your true presence exists; you are all-pervading, ever the wind; / no other deity is all-pervading except you, O breath of life! / And this world of living beings is sustained by you, O wind; / this world of living beings is directly evident to you, O source of life! / You know the lord, the god who is master of speech, director of the mind; / tell us in what place was that alteration of his form caused, and why! / Having heard the word of those seers of purified soul, / the wind-god, of great splendour, bowed to by the world, answered them. / The wind said:
Formerly in the Kṛta age, O brahmins, intent on ascertaining the Veda, / a righteous mind-born Prajāpati named Vasiṣṭha,

seated comfortably upon a delightful golden rock-slab, the destroyer of the body of Love, / the daughter of the mountain king, her armlets adorned with pure gems, addressed with words: // 8.114.60
The Goddess said:
O Lord, ruler of the past and future, whose ordinance is marked by the bull! / On your throat, O Mahādeva, there shines like a cloud, / not excessively harsh, auspicious, bright, resembling a mass of blue collyrium. / What is this glowing upon your throat, O God, destroyer of Kāma's body? / What is the reason or what is the cause by which this is dark blue, O Īśvara? / I wish to hear all this in truth, according to the proper way. // 61–62
Then, having heard the words of the goddess Pārvatī, Śaṅkara, dear to Pārvatī, / related an auspicious story. // 63
Maheśvara said:
Formerly, when the nectar was being churned in the Ocean of Milk by gods and Dānavas, / there arose in the beginning a dreadful poison possessing the brilliance of the fire of time. // 64
Risen like death at the end of time, having the splendour of the sun at the dissolution of an age, / flashing on all sides, like the sun at the destruction of the three worlds. // 65

“By whom has your sovereignty been stripped away, that you have come to me?
In the creation of creatures, no one exists here who could turn back my commands. // 8.114.70
Over the spiritual, the elemental, and the divine,
and over the ripening of the karma of creatures, you are ever able to hold sway. // 71
What is the business, or what is the cause, or whence has fear arisen,
on account of which you are agitated, like deer harassed by a lion? // 72
You ought quickly to explain all this properly.”
Having heard that speech of the great-souled Brahmā, // 73
they spoke, together with the seers—the gods, the lord of the Daityas, and the Dānavas:
“O Brahmā, as the great ocean was being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras, // 74
resembling a serpent or a black bee, like a dark blue raincloud,
a terrible poison appeared, radiating like the fire of cosmic dissolution, // 75
arisen like Death the Destroyer, radiating like the fire at the end of the yuga,
shining like the sun at the destruction of the three worlds, flashing on all sides, // 76
approaching as a massive conflagration of blazing fires.
Their faces despondent, all saw that great poison arisen. // 77
By that rising poison, radiant as the fire of Time,
Janārdana, whose body was red and fair, was burned and turned black. // 78
Seeing Janārdana, whose body was red and fair, turned black,
we, all terrified, have taken refuge in you alone, O Brahmā!”
Having heard the dreadful words of the gods and asuras, // 79
the grandfather of the worlds, Brahmā of great splendor, replied: // 8.114.80

7.12.m:
Then, delighted with that noble Brahmā, / I, honored by him with the highest devotion, spoke to the Grandfather: // 103
‘O Lord, ruler of the past and future, lord of beings, of great austerity, / what deed should be done by me for you, O brāhmaṇa of virtuous vows? Speak!’ / Having heard [my] words, Brahmā then replied, O lotus-eyed lady: // 104
Brahmā said: / ‘O lord of past, present, and future, listen, O lord of causes! / As the great ocean was being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras, O god, // 105
a dreadful poison appeared, resembling a peacock or a bee, like a dark cloud, / possessing a radiance like the cosmic fire of dissolution; // 106
arisen like the Death of Time, with the brilliance of the sun at the end of an age, / shining like the sun that destroys the three worlds, flashing on all sides. // 107 //’

‘By that rising poison, which has an intensity equal to the fire of cosmic dissolution, / Janārdana, whose limbs were reddish-fair, was scorched and turned black. // 108
Having seen Janārdana, whose limbs were reddish-fair, turned black, / we all, terrified, have sought refuge in you alone. // 109
Therefore drink it, O Mahādeva, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds! / You indeed are the consumer of the first portion; you are the lord, the foremost of the gods! // 110
You are capable of restraining its tremendous force; / no other person whatsoever in this world of moving and unmoving beings is able. // 111
You alone, O Mahādeva of great splendor, are able to drink / that which has a fierce power and an intensity equal to the fire of cosmic dissolution. // 112 //’

accepting his word, saying ‘So be it!’, O fair-faced lady, / I then began to drink that poison resembling Death, // 114

When that kālakūṭa poison of terrible fire was held in my throat, O daughter of the king of mountains, / all the host of gods and Daityas, watching, rejoiced and were filled with the highest wonder. // 120

7.12.m:
You alone are subtle, you the imperishable Person; you alone are subtle, and beyond the subtle, the most subtle; / you alone are the manifest, you alone the unmanifest nature; you alone are purity, and the origin of existence. // 124
You alone are earth, you alone water, you alone fire, and you alone wind; / you alone are space, past, present, and future; you alone are what has been, joined with what exists and is to come. // 125
You alone are sacrifice, you alone restraint; you alone perform all righteousness; / you alone are the separate apportioner of all that moves and is still, and its protector at the dissolution.” // 126
Having spoken these words, the chiefs of the gods and the hosts of the siddhas, rejoicing, bowed to me; / freed from sorrow, having received their share of soma, they departed in aerial chariots with the swift fury of the wind. // 127
This is the supreme mystery, exceedingly holy among holy things, / a great praise-hymn spoken by the Self-manifest [Brahmā] himself, destroying sin. // 128
Whoever constantly retains it, devoted to me and steadfast in restraint, / this auspicious [song] sung by Brahmā, which removes all diseases— // 129
I shall declare the destiny of that embodied soul both in the next world and in this. / For him, O fair-hipped lady, poison—both immobile and mobile— // 130
upon reaching the body, O beautifully rounded woman, is quickly rendered powerless; / it is pacified, bringing good fortune, and removes terrible nightmares. // 131
He becomes beloved among women and in the king's assembly; / in dispute he attains victory, and in battle as well—of this there is no doubt. // 132
Safety attends him as he journeys on the road, and strength arises in him. / When his body breaks up, I shall declare his destiny, O fair-faced woman: // 133

And whatever mortals, O fair-hipped lady, always hear this, / I shall tell you their fruit as well, O bestower of a thousand fruits: // 137
A brahmin obtains the Veda, a kṣatriya wins the earth, / a vaiśya gains profit, and a śūdra attains a good destiny. // 138
One who is diseased is freed from illness; one who is bound is freed from bonds; / a pregnant woman gives birth to a son; an unmarried girl wins a good husband. // 139
One recovers lost property in this world and in the next. / Whatever fruit comes from a hundred thousand cows given rightly, // 140
that very fruit a mortal attains by hearing this narrative, / whether a single syllable, a quarter-verse, a verse, or even half a verse. // 141

full of faith and ever diligent, he is honoured in the world of Rudra. / Recite it, O goddess, may you be blessed, and cause your kin to recite it! // 143

7.12.m:
Everything is achieved by him through the recitation of this hymn. / Having heard this supreme secret, even those of sinful birth, / women and Śūdras too, verily go to Rudra's realm in this world. / When, in the course of time, one ever attains human birth, / he is born in a pure family, knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas; / he becomes devoted to the gods and then practices dharma. / This holy story, destroying all sins, / has been told by me here, well-pleased, of my own accord, O lotus-eyed one!"
Thus in the Skandapurāṇa, in the story of Nīlakaṇṭha during the churning for nectar, the hundred and fourteenth chapter, entitled 'The Hymn to Mahādeva Composed by Lord Brahmā.'
Vyāsa said:
"When that nectar was stolen away by Viṣṇu in a disguised form, / what did the Daityas and Dānavas do immediately after that?"
Sanatkumāra said:
"Deceived by Viṣṇu, all those lords of the Dānavas, out of wrath, / then girded themselves for battle, and reviling Viṣṇu, they said: / 'Fie on your strength, and fie on your valor, you sinner! Fie on your prowess! / You are always a breaker of trust, a performer of base deeds, and wicked-souled! / By you, through treachery, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain long ago, / as was Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of Daityas; and this nectar was stolen away. / You have no strength in battle; indeed, you are strong only through deceit. / Just stand in battle! You shall not escape from us!'"

Sanatkumāra said:
"Then the king of the Daityas, enraged and emitting sparks of fire, / rushed directly at Viṣṇu with a chariot rumbling like a cloud.
And the Daitya lord Vipracitti, mounted on an elephant, / then challenged the thousand-eyed [Indra] who was armed with the thunderbolt and mounted on an elephant. / But Virocana, greatly enraged, rushed on an elephant / toward the lord of wealth [Kubera] and king of the Rākṣasas, like a cloud toward the sun. / And Bali, son of Virocana, rushed upon Yama, lord of the host of ancestors, / in a chariot, like one obstacle against another obstacle.
And Anuhrāda, the Daitya lord and son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, / rushed toward Varuṇa like the surge of a river toward the ocean.

7.12.m: Maya, the foremost of the Dānavas, and Tāra and Tāraka / clashed with the Ādityas, like elephants with great elephants. / Śarabha, Śataketu, Bala, and the Dānava Mūka / charged against the Rudras, like lions against lions in the wilderness. / Śambhu, Kārtasvana, and the great illusionist Śambara / clashed with the Vasus, like misfortunes with good men. / Then Naraka, Hayagrīva, and the Asura Indradamana / clashed with the two Aśvins, like planets with two stars. / And other Dānavas of great magical power and immense might, / challenging repeatedly, all fought in anger with other gods. / Vipracitti of great magical power, filling the ten directions with his roar, / afflicted the thousand-eyed [Indra] with three arrows.

Then a cry of woe arose in the army of the Dānavas, / while the cries of 'Well done, well done!' and lion-roars of the gods swelled. / Then, having regained consciousness, with a fierce spear / he dispatched his furious elephant to Yama's abode. / Then the foremost of the gods shattered his rear guards and resplendent armor; / abandoning the battle, he fled. / Bali [confronted] Yama's Puṇḍra, and Kṛtānta, Kalaha, / Kāla, Niyati, the servants, and the noose as well.

7.12.m:
Janārdana quickly severed that mace with his discus alone. / Then those valiant Dānavas, their prowess shattered by the gods, / broke in fear, just as herds of deer in the forest [scatter] before lions. / Seeing those [forces] broken and routed, they abandoned the battlefield and fled.
Prahlāda too left the battlefield and followed them. / When they were broken, then the highly revered cry of victory for Indra
was raised together by the gods along with Nārāyaṇa and the world-protectors; / they roared diverse lion-roars and sounded musical instruments. / Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter on the churning for nectar and the battle in the Skandapurāṇa.

Then, O Vyāsa, that imperishable one overran the three worlds with his might. / And that lord of the Asuras became the sovereign of the three worlds. / Having defeated the lord of the gods in battle, the powerful one displaced him from his position. / And having great strength, he assumed the role of Indra and the role of Yama; / he himself became Varuṇa, the lord of wealth [Kubera], and likewise Agni, / the sun, the moon, and Parjanya who releases the rain. / He himself constantly performs every duty to be done in the world.
While he was thus ruling the kingdom, there was misery for the gods at that time. / Deprived of their sovereignty, the great-souled ones wandered like birds. / To those grieving, great-souled ones, Brahmā gave counsel, / having comforted them in many ways out of compassion, O Vyāsa, being the best of gods. / Brahmā said: / “O gods, this Bali cannot be harassed by you. / He is high-souled, righteous, and immortal, without doubt, / devoted to brahmins, extremely strong, and one who has obtained boons.

[Critical apparatus and page number] / Assuming the form of a dwarf, let him ask for three strides of earth. / Having received that, he will give it; let this one stride in all directions.
He will make the entire earth equal to one stride, without doubt. / Then the Creator will personally [provide] his second stride in the atmosphere.

Sanatkumāra said: / Having been spoken to thus, the lords of the gods, having determined that it was very auspicious, / of great strength, said to Viṣṇu: “Let the word of Brahmā be carried out.
That best of Asuras has been consecrated today for a horse sacrifice. / Tomorrow is his concluding ritual bath; go and beg him, O Lord.”
Sanatkumāra said: / Having been told by him, “So be it,” the gods, clad in armor for battle, / all stood ready at that time, placing Śakra at their head.
Then Nārada went and was worshipped by him with devotion. / Comfortably seated, the best of speakers spoke these words:
“I am pleased with your righteousness, and so are the seers rich in austerity. / This conduct of yours, O best of Dānavas, is not like that of an Asura.
For all Dānavas are cruel, slayers of brahmins, and thorns in the side of the worlds; / but you are devoted to brahmins and a doer of good for the worlds.
Therefore your welfare should always be considered, O bull among the Asuras; / and, O King, in such a way that there may be some good for you.”

7.12.m:
If Madhusūdana, abandoning his own duty, / begs from me as a wretched soul, my life has attained its fruit. / And this is always my vow, O brahmin, O great sage: / being asked, I should never say, ‘I will not give,’ O Lord. / For the life-breaths of the beggar depart upwards, O best of brahmins; / but for the one who says ‘I will not give’, they depart downwards toward hell.
‘Give!’ is the sound of weeping; ‘There is none’ is answering with weeping. / Let other people not see me weeping, O Nārada! / This desire arises in every person, O great sage: / ‘This one is my giver!’ For the beggar, that [giver’s] fruit is imperishable.
If I, such as I am, do not give what is greatly begged by enemies, / I shall enter the hell named Raurava, without doubt. / For that vile person who does not give to one who asks / destroys that beggar by cutting off his hope, without doubt.

Vāmana said:
"This has always been your solemn vow, O best of Asuras: / 'Whatever a brahmin asks for, that I will give.' // 54

Sanatkumāra said:

Bali said:
"You are Viṣṇu in the form of a brahmin; disguised, you beg of me. / Abandoning the duty of a kṣatriya, you speak in helplessness. // 57
I would give to all who are wretched when requested; / excepting the kingdom, I will give you, a god, whatever you desire." // 58
Vāmana said:
"It is true, I am Viṣṇu; our kingdom was taken away by you. / Today we have no longing for a kingdom, for we are free from desire. / We ask you for a house, where I may dwell in peace." // 59
Bali said:
"What is the measure of that house you ask for, O lord of gods? / What is it like, and where shall I give it? Tell me everything, O Vāmana." // 60
Vāmana said:
"Endowed with all the qualities of the earth, wherever it may be, a great house / measuring three of my strides—give that, O king, to me who seeks a house." // 61

[…] Prahlāda said:
"What is this great deed you have resolved upon, my foolish son?
It will bring about the ruin of the sons of Diti; this must not be done, O mighty one!
This is Viṣṇu himself, master of great illusion, wicked-minded slayer of the Daityas.
He will indeed stride over the three worlds; of this there is no doubt.
You are our refuge, my son; you are our strength, you are our prowess.
Our very life depends on you; do not bring about our swift destruction!
King Hiraṇyakaśipu and the Dānava Hiraṇyākṣa
did not equal even a sixteenth part of you, O king, my son.

Do not give a dwelling to this deity, I tell you.
For this is the welfare of all, and of yourself, O mighty one!"
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the high-souled Prahlāda,
the righteous and illustrious Bali bowed and spoke as follows:
Bali said:
"I know that this deity is Viṣṇu, the terminator of all Asuras.
Yet this is indeed my vow: what is asked of me must be given.
I am renowned as a master of giving, famed throughout the three worlds.
How could I act otherwise while life remains, O Dānavas?
It is unrighteous, disgraceful, unheavenly, and brings great terror.
How indeed could I speak an untruth? Such is the vow I have undertaken.
Having promised, how again could [...] for the sake of righteousness?"
Prahlāda said:
"The duty of the Dānavas and Daityas, my son, has been forged by themselves.
For the Diti-born Dānavas always prosper by unrighteousness.

and the robbery of sacrifices—this indeed is our beneficial duty.
Therefore, though having promised, O mighty one, do not give to that wicked soul!
For thus our growth will be ensured; otherwise there is great peril here."

its fruit is not eternal, O best of Asuras, for it is cruel.

King Hiraṇyakaśipu did not attain enduring happiness,
nor did Hiraṇyākṣa, nor Andhaka his son;
nor did you, our grandfather, through such cruel deeds.
Therefore, whatever wise men there are do not praise this.
Behold the seers established in heaven through truth and righteousness!
The gods conquer exceedingly, and the planets shine forth.
No one is seen in the sky through such cruel action.
Propitiating you and seeking your pardon, I speak, O lord of Diti's children."
Prahlāda said:
"Whether corrupt or cruel, or whether auspicious, O Dānava,
one's own duty, handed down from generation to generation, should never be abandoned.
[...] Practiced by the fathers and grandfathers,
this, my son, should not be abandoned by you, O great sage!"
Bali said:
"As it was practiced unhesitatingly by our fathers as duty,
yet was condemned by the virtuous, listen to me, O grandfather.

7.12.m:
There was a noble seer known as Vāmadeva.
Seeing Urvaśī, his seed fell from passion.
Cast upon the ground, a mare swallowed it.
A pregnancy arose in her, and she presently gave birth to a female mule.
Out of affection for his child, that seer raised her for many years.
Then the valorous royal sage named Aṣṭaka arrived there.
He saw her, O best of kings, standing in the middle of the seer's hermitage,
and, exceedingly delighted, thought this in his heart:
'She equals my wife in her wealth of auspicious marks.
If the brahmin should give her to me, my union would be supreme.

Yet this brahmin will not give me this very rare creature.
I shall employ a stratagem by which he will bestow the radiant one.'
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that king went and spoke to Vāmadeva,
bowing with great respect, yet deceitfully, O son of Śakti.
The king said:
'I have some business with this female mule, O great sage.
Being requested, grant her [to me] for a full year.
When the task is complete, to you indeed, O best of twice-born,
I will give her back again, O prince of brahmins, if she may be given, let her be given!'
Then that tiger among seers gave the blameless one to him.
Taking her, the king departed, delighted that she was obtained.
Then, when the year had elapsed, the best of seers said to him—
then the brahmin said to him: 'Return the auspicious female mule!'"

Infuriated with anger, that brahmin addressed him likewise: / "I shall destroy the entire family of evil-minded Aṣṭaka!"
Hearing his words, the boy worshipped the twice-born and said: / "After consulting the ministers, I will give the female steed later." / Having summoned the ministers then, O lord of the Dānavas, he asked: / "Speak! Should this auspicious mule be given or not?" / The ministers said: / "Formerly, O king, this mule was brought here by your great-grandfather / after begging [the loan of her] for one year.
When the year was complete, though the brahmin asked, O great sage, / she was not given, and by the anger of this brahmin he died.
Then your grandfather became king, O lord of subjects; / likewise he did not give her, and died through the brahmin's anger.
If you follow the conduct of your ancestors, / she should not be given to this evil-minded death in the form of a brahmin."

Then, seeing that most difficult act of his, all the seers rich in austerity, / praising the lord of the sons of Diti, bowed low before Madhusūdana. / Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the Vāmana [story].
Sanatkumāra said: / Then the blessed Lord Viṣṇu said to the foremost of the asuras: / "Behold, O radiant lord of the Dānavas, I shall stride out with my strides! / If what has been given is sufficient, [well and good]; if not, / another portion of land must be given by you: be true to your word, O Dānava!" / Bali said: / "Stride out completely, O best of Vāmanas, with your three strides today! / If it is not sufficient, I am the giver; I tell you this as truth!" / Sanatkumāra said: / Then, about to stride, the imperishable Viṣṇu bowed with supreme devotion / to the lord of the gods, Mahādeva, the consort of Umā.

Thus addressed, having taken leave of him, he entered Pātāla. / The gods too, having obtained their own kingdom, rejoiced exceedingly.
Vyāsa said: / Of what nature was the blessed Viṣṇu when, abandoning his mighty dharma, / he took back the three worlds, and yet no injustice accrued to him?
Sanatkumāra said: / As he was taking his strides, the form of that god Viṣṇu, / radiant as blazing fire, shone exceedingly fiercely, hard even for the gods to gaze upon.
Then the gods together with Indra, their purpose accomplished, praised / and extolled the supreme deity Viṣṇu of mighty strength.
Filled with supreme joy, all bearing divine missiles, [said]: / "When we were being oppressed by the dānavas, [you became] the lord of the gods, / our protector, and the bestower of the kingdom, O best among deities! / Through you we are all made happy, as doers of good deeds are by their merits.

Then, out of that conceit, O sage, his supreme yoga
perished, just as fire sprinkled with water. (29)
Then, finding that opening, O sage, that demonic evil,
greatly delighted, entered Janārdana. (30)
Possessed by that evil, O Vyāsa, the imperishable Viṣṇu
did not shine with radiance there, like a good man falling into cruel misfortune. (31)
Thus ends the one hundred seventeenth chapter, on the striding across the three worlds in the Vāmana narrative, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Because this friend of the gods, the great-souled Vaikuṇṭha,
having abandoned his own duty, accepted the gift of the kingdom, (10)
therefore the evil of the asuras, terrifying to all living beings,
having abandoned the asuras, entered Keśava. (11)

and do you not all see that his splendour is not auspicious as before?" (12)

in that same way, O bird, understand the action of the tree as born of its nature; / abandon this and go elsewhere, wherever there may be comfort."
The parrot said: / "I am not a fool, O ruler of the gods! Do not despise my words; / listen to my wisdom, O lord of the gods, O mighty one!
Fire, water, and wind are truly insentient; / but not so trees, shrubs, creepers, and the like, O tiger among gods.
For this cycle of existence is ordained for all beings that perform actions; / therefore, insentience does not belong to trees, O ruler of the gods.
And listen to this from me, as to how trees have the thought: / 'How may we in every way bring about benefit to living beings?'
The self-manifest, renowned one, having created these chief [plants], said to them: / 'Act in every way for the benefit of living creatures!'
Therefore, through fruits, flowers, bark, sprouts, and even down to their very core, / they act for the benefit of all living beings, O protector of the world."

Then, O great sage, all those gods went indeed to the city named Kṛmilā, / and there they saw this:
There was a brahmin woman named Gautamī, like another Rudrāṇī, / virtuous and generous, whose sins had been burnt away by austerity.
While she was intent on austerity, her husband having gone to the world of Brahmā, / her son was bitten by a great black serpent and died.
A hunter named Arjunaka arrived at that place; / having come, he then saw him overwhelmed with poison.

"What do you gain by binding me? Do you not see the unrighteousness? / We are not even food for mortals; why do you not release me?" (9)
Arjuna said: / "Cutting you into pieces today, I will give you as food to a peacock; / because this son of a seer, bitten by you, has died." (10)
The serpent said: / "Impelled by Time, I bit that young son of a seer; / you ought not in truth to cast fault upon me, O Arjunaka." (11)
Arjuna said: / "Even if impelled by Time you bit him, O snake, / you are indeed the instrumental cause in his death; therefore, I will surely slay you." (12)
Sanatkumāra said: / Then that Gautamī, O Vyāsa, made an invocation against Time and Death; / afflicted with supreme sorrow, Time, terrified, approached then. (13)
Time said: / "I am indeed the Time of all living beings; there is no doubt about this; / impelled by Death alone, I killed the young son of a seer." (14)

7.12.m:
The conjunction of living beings with a body is brought about by virtue and vice, O auspicious lady; / and their separation from the body occurs again through the exhaustion of both.
Virtue alone is declared to be the cause of the lifespan of embodied beings; / upon its exhaustion, death is proclaimed, and that is remembered as Time and Death.
In the Kṛta age, Time is said to be four thousand years; / in the Tretā, three thousand; in the Dvāpara, two thousand.
In the Kali age, however, they declare the lifespan of a living being to be only a hundred years, O lady of great vows. / From that [span], untimely death is declared as something else; hear also about that death:
The gods who dwell in the senses of a person, O best of the two-legged, / all those foremost deities take away a portion of his life:
when he looks upon what is corrupt with his eye, and likewise when he speaks what is corrupt; / when he hears, conceives, perceives, and looks upon [what is corrupt];

And the spirits take another portion from one who behaves very evilly toward them; / and diseases take another portion;
the ancestors take another portion, and the gods take another after that; / and the seers, the fire, the moon and sun, and the planets take another.
Thus, O virtuous lady, to whatever extent [life] is snatched away from that embodied being, / for just so long may he live; and that is declared to be untimely death.

Then, O virtuous lady, a disease manifests and cuts into the vital spots. / With his vital spots severed, helpless, having abandoned the body, O lady of great vows,
and having obtained another body, he enters another destiny. / If, however, through the favor of the gods residing in the body, that vice does not inflict disease upon him,
it certainly slays him by another means: / by poison, weapons, falling, diverse creatures, / and many other dreadful ways; there is no fault in the one who clearly sees this."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having seen this through her austerity, that Gautamī of very great vows, / free from sorrow, spoke these words to that hunter Arjunaka:

Gautamī said:
"Release him, Arjunaka! This serpent does not deserve to be killed. / Possessed by vice and by the deities, he bit my son.

The gods said:
"We are pleased with you, O knower of righteousness, whose sins are burned away by austerity. / Let this son of yours live and abide in his own duty.

Indeed, this test was made of you by these gods, O lady of great vows. / All the worlds will be imperishable for you, without a doubt."

Sanatkumāra said:
Then those gods headed by Indra immediately / beheld what had occurred there, and I reported all of that.
Having bathed, they went again, collected in mind, to another sacred ford, / all those greatly fortunate ones, and likewise to others again and again.
Wandering in succession, they came again to [the place of] the Kṛtyā, / where the Kṛtyā was previously slain by the lord of gods of great majesty.
Vyāsa said:
"By whom was that Kṛtyā produced, for what purpose, and of whom, O lord? / And how was she slain again? I wish to know this."
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a king of great might known as Tṛṇabindu. / Skilled in speech, he addressed these words to the seven sages:
"Perform a sacrifice for me, O brahmins; I will give you abundant wealth." / They replied: "We will not sacrifice for you, O good ruler of men."
When that noble-minded king was consecrated by another during a drought, / they, afflicted by hunger, arrived at the sacrifice by chance.

Then the king said to them: "Speak, what may I give to you?" / With wrathful faces they replied: "Give us your son, O ruler of the earth!"
Having honoured them, that king gave [them] both his son and wealth,
bowing down with great respect, O son of Parāśara.
As he bowed in this manner, those rich in austerity left the wealth behind
and departed taking the son; [yet] that boy, due to his delicacy,
afflicted there by hunger and thirst and by the journey, died indeed.
Leaving him in a forest fire, they stood watching.

7.12.m:
As they were watching there, O Vyāsa, the king arrived.
Laughing, his earrings radiant, he spoke this to those seers:
Tṛṇabindu said:
“You did not accept a gift from me, O rich in austerity,
nor do you, sages thrived on austerity, perform sacrifices for us.
Do you not see sin in the death of this child here, O brahmins?
In an unrighteous and dishonourable act—ah, great indeed is your regard for righteousness!”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, disregarding him and saying nothing at all,
they went in another direction, O Vyāsa, sorely tormented by hunger in the forest.
And Tṛṇabindu then, by his austerity, created many trees right at that moment,
O Vyāsa, desiring their comfort and welfare.
Reaching that forest, they saw many trees laden with fruit,
O Vyāsa, and they experienced supreme contentment.
Plucking and breaking [the fruits], they then saw inside them
gold, cooked food, eatables, and also radiant silver.

7.12.m:
Those possessed of austerity considered that to have been made by Tṛṇabindu.
Then those seven seers of good vows abandoned that forest
and set out in another direction; and Tṛṇabindu grew angry.
Going to those seers, bowed down with joined palms,
his mind overcome with sorrow and agitated, that king spoke:
Tṛṇabindu said:
“I am certainly not fallen, O brahmins, nor of wicked deeds,
nor forsaken by brahmins, nor one who does not sacrifice, nor an evildoer.
I am born in a pure lineage of kings, O rich in austerity;
I protect the subjects properly. Why do you not respect me highly?”
Hearing that speech of his, those seers of great vows
said: “We will by no means accept a gift from you, O king.
You are excellent, endowed with virtues, a protector of subjects, a lord of subjects.
We are pleased; we do not accept wealth from you, O lord of the earth.”

7.12.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing their fault in their going away, O Vyāsa, Purandara
arrived in the guise of a wandering mendicant, accompanied by a dog.
Seeing him laughing, the long-armed one with a triple staff in hand,
they all spoke quietly to one another.
The seers said:
“Surely this man eats day and night without wearying,
and from that he has become fat here.
Or else his palm is always outstretched as a perpetual beggar,
a seller of austerity and sacred study—therefore has he grown fat.”
Having conjectured about him in many ways, those seers rich in austerity
addressed that great-souled one, asking: “Who are you?”
Indra said:
“I am a wandering mendicant, O best of brahmins, coming from Daśeraka.
I am going to the auspicious reservoir; my name is Śunassakha.

Sanatkumāra said:
Then together with him they went to the auspicious lotus-pool.
They saw that kṛtyā and were stopped by her:
“If you wish to plunge into this, O brahmins,
tell your names and then proceed in comfort without harm.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then they said to that maiden: “Let it be so.”
And Śvasakha, the tamer of foes, spoke thus to all those seers:
“O brahmins, this is a demoness, not an ordinary mortal;
for this matter must be dealt with according to what she tells you.
If you wish for the highest, beneficial good,
then declare your names in such a way that she cannot understand them.”

Sanatkumāra said:
Saying “Let it be so,” O Vyāsa, those auspicious sages
recited their names to her and entered [the water] as they wished.
They spoke their own names etymologically and hard to comprehend,
which that kṛtyā did not understand; then they entered the water.
Sanatkumāra said:
Not comprehending their names, she who was born of the flame
said to Śvasakha: “Speak, and then you may go, or not!”
Śvasakha said:
“I am the friend of dogs, O cruel one, and I associate with dogs;
know me therefore as Śvasakha, O demoness, night-wanderer!”
The demoness said:
“Say your name just once again, O lowest of mortals;
then, known to me, you may go near the brahmins.”
Śvasakha said:
“I am the lord, the friend of dogs; my friendship with dogs never departs.
As Śvasakha, I strike you down, O demoness—behold!”

Then, having arrived there, the gods and the seers rich in austerities

Then, having approached the Himavat mountain, filled with joy,
those of noble vows caused Viṣṇu to perform the horse-sacrifice.
While he was sacrificing, Tryambaka, lord of the gods, along with the lords of his gaṇas,
arrived through the sky toward the sacrifice, filled with delight.
Vyāsa said:
Oh, indeed, this narrative of the female demon has been told to me by you,
O son of Brahmā—a supreme secret, most difficult to know.
For this is a supreme secret, endowed with great meaning, ever conferring renown and supremely purifying,
set forth properly by you, O master of great yoga, like the nectar of old, radiant as the full moon.
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, the narrative of the female demon in the pilgrimage of Vāmana's sacred ford, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Vyāsa said:
Beyond this, tell us how that blessed supreme lord went
after having seen him who was sacrificing with the sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said:
That spear-wielding deity, the blessed one whose emblem is a bull,
spoke thus to the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight:
'O goddess, O blessed one, today in the world is the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight;
tonight we two shall go to observe the cremation grounds.'
Devī said:
'As it pleases you, O god, O protector of the world, let it be so;
whatever is dear to you, O Mahādeva, is twice as dear to me.'

7.12.m:
'O brahmins, O men, listen to my words that I speak to you;
you are clearly devoid of sense; hear my counsel!
He has died indeed through time; why do you grieve like fools?
He will not live because of crying; attend to your own welfare, free from distress.'
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard his words, they then abandoned the son and began to leave,
looking back again and again. Then a jackal said to them:
'Oh, shame! All you men, look, you who are devoid of wisdom!
Unloving and ungrateful, how can you leave him and go?
With difficulty is a son obtained, and so too is he born;
and with difficulty, O cruel ones, does he grow up, afflicted by illness!
Have you forgotten indeed all those exceedingly many charming words
which this boy spoke? Oh, the lovelessness in you!'
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having heard the jackal's words, O Vyāsa, they returned,
and surrounding [the body] and weeping, they remained then in the cemetery.

"O God, eight hundred and sixteen thousand / divine years of the battle of the gods have elapsed. / Both Tāraka and Maya, Dānavas maddened by war— / taking refuge in them both, all the Asuras are slaughtering the gods like beasts.
To those gods who are being slain, O best of gods, / grant life, or whatever, O God, is fitting."

7.12.m:
Since those sons of Siṃhikā have suddenly been slain by you,
that great deed belongs only to you, or to Tryambaka at Tripura.
There is no one equal to you in the world; I speak this truly.
They could not be equaled by any god or by any mortal;
though invulnerable to all living beings, they were slaughtered by you alone.
Therefore, pleased with you, we grant you invulnerability,
inexhaustible strength in battle, and supreme fame on earth.
And Tryambaka will approach you with desired divine boons,
and you shall conquer the host in battles as you desire.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus spoken to by those pleased gods, O Vyāsa, that ascetic of great austerities,
the renunciant with a gladdened and delighted mind, went to the god Tryambaka.
The gods, too, well-prepared, then swiftly rushed upon
Tāraka, who was maddened by war, together with Maya.
Those mighty ones, their fury held back by the onslaught of the Daityas, yet rushing with the speed of an ocean,
fell upon the hordes of Daityas and struck them violently, as forest lions strike elephants.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, named “The Bestowal of Boons on the Son of Jamadagni,” in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.12.m:
Vipracitti, Ṣaṇḍa, and the great Asura Prahlāda.
Then, enraged, Kālanemi advanced against Keśava in battle.
Mounting a great chariot equipped with a raised banner a hundred nalvas high,
the Dānava rushed with speed against Keśava.
Even as he charged, Keśava loosed his great, unhindered discus, O Vyāsa;
he then obstructed it.
Seeing it obstructed, all the gods became enraged;
disarmed, they were indeed defeated by Kālanemi.
[…]
Having routed them, the lord of Daityas turned them away,
and having done so, the imperishable one then assumed the status of World-Protector.
Pervading the earth and heaven at that time, existing as one of great power,
like the Self-manifest one, he wandered through the three worlds by worldly illusion.
Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing that Daitya established in such a state, the gods along with Indra,
terrified with fear, then took refuge with the imperishable Hari.
And Hari, the refuge, the lord of the gods and friend of the three worlds,
granted them freedom from fear, desiring the death of the Dānava.

Pervading heaven and earth in every way with his cosmic form at that time,
he remembered that lotus-marked discus which had been fashioned by Rudra.
Then with it, O Vyāsa, he struck off the great head of the Dānava,
as a violent wind knocks down a ripe fruit from the top of a palmyra palm.
When that Daitya was slain, both Tāraka and Maya,
the great warriors, retreated and rushed swiftly toward Pātāla.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, O Vyāsa, took place that fierce battle [against the sickness] caused by Tāraka,
in which Kālanemi was slain, along with the renowned Virocana,
the valiant sons of Siṃhikā, the great Asura Tuhuṇḍa,
Surocana, Śatāvarta, Hāla, and Gārgyaśiras,

Vipāka along with Pāka, Caṇḍa, Kārtasvana, and Kubha.
These and other lords of Daityas were slain in [that war against] Tāraka’s sickness.
And at the battle of the banner, the cruel Vipracitti was slain with his younger brother.
Vyāsa said:
How did that battle take place between the gods and the Asuras,
and how did its name come to be “Dhvaja” (Banner)?
And after performing that deed difficult for all beings,
the descendant of Bhrgu’s line, the son of Jamadagni, came into the presence of Tryambaka.
What was he told by the god of gods? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said:
Sent by the immortals themselves at that time, Jamadagni’s son
went to Puriścandra, the secret dwelling of the god.

7.12.m:
Vyāsa said:
How did that celestial dwelling, Puriścandra,
become the secret abode of the Great Lord? Relate that, O one of steadfast vows.
Sanatkumāra said:
Here I shall relate to you an ancient event, O wise one,
hearing which even an evildoer may attain the supreme destination.
Formerly there were two seers of great soul, Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
for the sake of the gods' purpose, it is said, they committed the slaying of a brahmin.
Overcome by that evil deed, those two extraordinarily powerful gods
lost their senses and fell severely into animal wombs.
Then, when a divine year had elapsed, the boundless-minded
Brahmā himself arrived there along with the gods and the seers.

Saying, "So be it," the lords of the gods, lying in the water
together with the seers, chanted for six million years. // 29
Then, after a great span of time, for those of composed self,
subtle yoga appeared, from which an auspicious fire arose. // 30

Nara and Nārāyaṇa and entered into the water. // 31
The waters, entered by it, did not remain sapid; they lost their taste,
they became devoid of fragrance, discolored, and bereft of luster;
the earth became devoid of strength, and heat lost its sharpness. // 32
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, seeing it thus, they again applied themselves [in yoga]
and chanted the Rudrahṛdaya with concentrated minds. // 33

and said to the gods: "I am pleased; speak of what you desire." // 34

“O gods, I am well pleased; choose the boon you desire!
I shall grant it, O greatly wise ones; do not remain silent, speak out in full!”
The gods said:
“This Hari, O Mahādeva, has his mind afflicted by sin.
Dispel it swiftly from him, like the sun [dispelling] mist!
For the benefit of the world and for the sake of the gods, this mighty one
performs deeds, O Lord of gods; destroy, therefore, his sin!”

7.12.m:
“And may we, dwelling among the attendants, attain equality with you,
the status of attendants, O Lord of all gods, if you deem it proper, O All-pervading One!”
Sanatkumāra said:
While those gods were speaking thus, O best of seers,
the blessed Śarva, laughing with a delighted heart, spoke:
“This Viṣṇu, O gods, shall immediately be released from this sin,
and this sin, O blessed ones, shall come into existence in saline soil,
and in the sap of trees, and in the foam of waters,
and in the smell of great serpents, and likewise in the reviling of women,
and in proclaiming the inauspicious misfortune of an initiated brahmin,
in slander of brahmins, and in failing to praise cows,
and in not kindling the fire, and in the damming of rivers.
Whatever man, filled with passion and delusion, should do these things,
he would incur this [sin] in the world, even if he were a self-manifest guardian of the world.
When, however, Viṣṇu becomes the son of Vasudeva,
then this Nara shall enjoy her in bodily form.

he, completely freed from sin, shall then walk this world again.

7.12.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by the God, all the gods then said to Hari:
“Perform severe austerity; from that you will indeed attain the highest good.”
Then he, ascending Candra, king of mountains, deeply concentrated,
performed immense austerity, mortifying the host of senses.
The noble gods also, together with the seers of noble vows,
deeply concentrated, performed austerity on Hiraṇyavarṇa, king of mountains.
Then, when their observance was concluded, the wielder of the Pināka
enjoined that blazing, great Pāśupata observance.
With a pleased heart, having addressed the bulls among gods,
he spoke in a voice deep and grave like the sound of clouds and kettledrums.
The God of gods said:
“This preparatory rite has been well performed by you yourself, O world-guardians;
having observed this Pāśupata [vow], go, untroubled and free from fear!
This supreme and purifying observance is superior to Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
nothing higher than this, nor more subtle, exists anywhere.

7.12.m:
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, sky-clad and pure,
worshipping Rudra with steadfastness of body, one is freed from all sins.
